classification.difficultyReason: Explain the supplied formula by excluding adjacent vertices and correcting double counting, then reverse the quadratic relationship. The interval task additionally requires locating and checking neighbouring integer side counts rather than merely substituting into the formula.

content.prompt: A diagonal of a polygon is a line segment joining a vertex to a non-adjacent vertex. In the diagram opposite, $AD$ is a diagonal of the polygon $ABCDE$.

spec.description: Unshaded convex pentagon with cyclic vertices A, B, C, D, E; EA is horizontal. Only diagonal AD is drawn, dashed and red. Ordinary source-blue boundary lines become black under house style.
spec.mathematics: AD joins two non-adjacent vertices of pentagon ABCDE.
spec.answerVisibility: All geometry and labels are permanent givens.

answer.worked: Each of the 4 vertices joins to 1 non-adjacent vertex. Each diagonal is counted twice, so the number of diagonals is $4\times1\div2=2$.
Each of the 5 vertices joins to 2 non-adjacent vertices. Dividing by 2 to avoid counting each diagonal twice gives $5\times2\div2=5$ diagonals.
Each of the 6 vertices joins to 3 non-adjacent vertices. Dividing by 2 to avoid counting each diagonal twice gives $6\times3\div2=9$ diagonals.
Each of the 10 vertices joins to 7 non-adjacent vertices. Dividing by 2 to avoid counting each diagonal twice gives $10\times7\div2=35$ diagonals.
Each of the 20 vertices joins to 17 non-adjacent vertices. Dividing by 2 to avoid counting each diagonal twice gives $20\times17\div2=170$ diagonals.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why the number of diagonals in an $n$-sided polygon is $\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$.

answer.short: Each of the $n$ vertices joins to $n-3$ non-adjacent vertices. Each diagonal is counted twice, so there are $\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$ diagonals.
answer.worked: From each vertex, exclude the vertex itself and its two adjacent vertices, leaving $n-3$ possible diagonal endpoints. Across all $n$ vertices this gives $n(n-3)$ counts. Every diagonal is counted from both endpoints, so divide by 2: $\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: A particular polygon has 405 diagonals. How many sides does it have?

answer.worked:
Let $n$ be the number of sides.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{n(n-3)}{2}&=405\\n(n-3)&=810\\n^2-3n-810&=0\\(n-30)(n+27)&=0\\n&=30\text{ or }n=-27\end{align*}$$
The number of sides is positive, so the polygon has 30 sides. Check: $30\times27\div2=405$ diagonals.

children.label: d
children.prompt: What polygon has between 1900 and 2000 diagonals?

answer.short:
A 64-gon.

Use $\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$ and check neighbouring whole numbers of sides.
answer.worked:
Let $D(n)=\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$ be the number of diagonals. As the whole number $n$ increases, the number of diagonals increases. Since $n(n-3)$ is near $4000$ and $\sqrt{4000}$ is near 63, test nearby whole numbers:
$$\begin{align*}D(63)&=\frac{63\times60}{2}=1890\\D(64)&=\frac{64\times61}{2}=1952\\D(65)&=\frac{65\times62}{2}=2015\end{align*}$$
Only 1952 is between 1900 and 2000, so the polygon is a 64-gon.
